lessons.text: Treat compilation, lint, and synthesis as necessary but insufficient: run a focused self-test before submitting, especially after behavioral changes.
Build tests from the specification’s corner cases, not just typical operation; check control-signal priority, reset behavior, stalls, and boundary conditions.
Use the interface documentation and existing instantiations to verify every required port, parameter, width, and connection before implementing or changing a module.
When a hidden test exposes a behavioral bug, trace the exact failing condition and add a regression for it; do not rely on a broad implementation plan alone.
For arithmetic and counters, verify operand widths, signedness, overflow, and wraparound explicitly rather than assuming the language infers the intended behavior.
For asynchronous or buffered designs, test empty/full transitions, simultaneous activity, pointer wraparound, and data integrity across clock domains.
If repeated tool checks fail, inspect the first diagnostic and resolve the underlying build issue before spending more turns on speculative edits.
Treat the first compile or lint failure as a blocker: inspect the full diagnostic, fix its root cause, and rerun the exact failing check before making more changes.

Read the specification and existing implementation before editing. Trace how the changed logic connects to surrounding modules, reset behavior, and handshakes instead of patching from a guessed symptom.
Preserve specified module interfaces and any externally observed hierarchy, signal, and parameter names; verify them against the spec before submitting.
Test the behavior hidden tests are likely to exercise, not just syntax: cover reset, boundary cases, transaction completion, and interactions across module boundaries.
Run a focused self-check after each meaningful change, then run the full available checks. A passing compile or a narrow test does not establish functional correctness.

When a test fails, use its first failing assertion to trace the expected behavior through the design and integration; do not assume a locally plausible implementation satisfies the system-level contract.
Use the available turn budget to converge: prefer a small, reviewable change and reserve time for a final compile, lint, and relevant behavioral test.
Treat the specification’s interface as exact: preserve required ports, parameters, module names, and any hierarchy the testbench may inspect.
Derive behavior from the specification and existing design conventions; do not assume standard defaults or address and state interpretations.
Resolve compile and lint failures before submission. A passing synthesis run or local testbench does not make other build failures safe to ignore.
Make self-checks exercise boundary cases, reset and recovery, and simultaneous or invalid operations—not just typical successful transactions.
Keep required source-file and submodule organization intact, and verify the design with the same kinds of build checks the submission harness is likely to use.
Work incrementally: make a focused change, run the relevant checks, and fix the first failure before adding more changes.
Budget time for validation; repeated failed tool runs without narrowing the cause are less useful than a minimal fix followed by a targeted test.
Treat synthesis failures as unresolved defects, even when compilation and lint pass. Do not submit until every required build check succeeds or you understand and justify a tool limitation.

Build a self-checking testbench before submission. Exercise the full behavioral contract, including corner cases, reset, stalls, and each supported operation—not just compilation or a few typical inputs.
When a self-check fails, use the failing case to isolate the defect, then rerun the complete test suite after each fix. Do not submit with a known failing test.
For arithmetic and encoding logic, test boundary values and combinations that challenge ordering, alignment, signedness, rounding, and special cases against an independent reference.

Read the specification and existing project structure before editing. Preserve required interfaces, hierarchy, and externally inspected internal objects unless the task explicitly permits changing them.
Keep changes focused, and verify that reset behavior, handshakes, and state updates match the stated timing and polarity conventions.
Manage time for validation: reserve turns for resolving build and test failures rather than spending the entire budget on implementation.
Read the specification and interface tables before editing. Preserve exact port names, widths, parameters, and expected hierarchy; hidden tests may access them directly.
For a repair task, trace the existing implementation and its dependencies before changing it. Make the smallest targeted fix rather than rewriting surrounding logic.
Use related, working designs as references for protocol conventions, but verify that their behavior matches the current specification.
Treat compile, lint, and synthesis failures as blockers. Resolve warnings or tool incompatibilities that indicate questionable RTL before submitting.
Build self-checks around protocol corner cases, not just typical transfers: independent handshakes, backpressure, reset, simultaneous events, and boundary conditions.
After the final edit, rerun the checks and testbench. A passing test from before the last change does not validate the submitted design.
Check timing and accounting carefully: verify when state updates occur and that events arriving together, or while output is blocked, are neither lost nor duplicated.
Treat compiler and linter failures as blockers: inspect the first diagnostic, make a focused correction, and rerun checks before attempting further RTL changes.
Turn the specification and any failure description into a precise cycle-by-cycle expectation; do not rely on a plausible diagnosis without checking the surrounding control logic.
Run a focused testbench for the reported behavior, then add cases for reset, stalls, boundary conditions, and competing transactions where relevant.
Check timing as well as values: verify when state and counters advance, especially around valid/ready handshakes and phase transitions.
After the final edit, rerun compilation and the relevant tests; earlier passing checks do not validate later changes.
